prompt: Some people think that universities should provide graduates with the knowledge and skills needed in the workplace. Others think that the true function of a university should be to give access to knowledge for its own sake. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
essay:
Nowadays there is a debate about the purpose of universities. Some people believe universities should prepare students for work, while others believe they should give knowledge for its own sake. In this essay I will discuss both views.

On the one hand, many people think universities must give practical skills. This is because the job market is very competitive and employers want graduates who can start working immediately. For example, engineering students need to know how to use modern software. If universities do not teach this, graduates will have problems to find a job.

On the other hand, some people think knowledge is valuable in itself. They say that studying subjects like history or philosophy helps people to think better. These subjects do not give a job directly but they make society better.

In my opinion, universities should do both things. They should teach practical skills but also give students the chance to study what they are interested in. In conclusion, both views have good points and a balance is the best solution.

prompt: Some people think that universities should provide graduates with the knowledge and skills needed in the workplace. Others think that the true function of a university should be to give access to knowledge for its own sake. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
essay:
The purpose of higher education is a subject of ongoing debate. While some argue that universities exist primarily to prepare students for employment, others maintain that their real value lies in the pursuit of knowledge itself. This essay will examine both positions before explaining why I believe the two aims are compatible.

Those who favour a vocational approach point to the cost of a degree and the expectations of employers. Students, particularly those from lower-income families, take on considerable debt, and it is reasonable for them to expect that their qualification will improve their employment prospects. Universities that ignore this risk producing graduates who are well read but unemployable, which benefits neither the individual nor the economy.

The opposing view holds that reducing education to job training is short-sighted. Disciplines such as philosophy and pure mathematics rarely lead to immediate employment, yet they develop analytical habits that transfer widely. Moreover, many of the most significant scientific advances began as research with no obvious application.

In my view, this is a false choice. A well-designed degree can teach transferable analytical skills through demanding academic content, and the graduates most valued by employers are usually those who can think independently rather than those trained in a single software package. Universities should therefore resist the pressure to become purely vocational institutions while remaining aware of what their graduates will face.

note: Sophisticated, precise, well-controlled; natural idiom and cohesion.
prompt: Some people think that universities should provide graduates with the knowledge and skills needed in the workplace. Others think that the true function of a university should be to give access to knowledge for its own sake. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
essay:
Debates about the purpose of the university tend to be framed as a contest between utility and enquiry: either institutions equip graduates for the labour market, or they preserve knowledge as an end in itself. The framing is convenient but misleading, and it obscures what universities have historically done well.

The vocational case is easy to state and difficult to dismiss. Where degrees are expensive and largely debt-financed, graduates are entitled to ask what their investment returns, and governments funding the system are entitled to ask the same. Fields with clear professional pathways, from medicine to civil engineering, are structured around precisely this expectation, and nobody seriously argues that a surgeon should be educated without regard to whether the operation succeeds.

Yet the disinterested pursuit of knowledge has a defence that is practical rather than merely romantic. The applications of a discovery are frequently invisible at the moment it is made: number theory was a byword for uselessness until it became the basis of modern cryptography. A system that funds only what can justify itself in advance systematically forecloses returns it cannot yet imagine.

My own position is that the opposition dissolves under examination. What employers consistently report wanting is not familiarity with a particular tool, which dates within years, but the capacity to structure an unfamiliar problem and to argue from evidence — capacities that are cultivated precisely by sustained engagement with difficult material for its own sake. The university that pursues understanding rigorously produces employable graduates as a by-product; the one that chases employability directly tends to achieve neither.
